title: Stablecoin regulation has outpaced global coordination. The G20 can help.
gist: Jai Massari argues that fragmented stablecoin regimes—the US GENIUS Act, the EU's MiCA, and a growing patchwork worldwide—leave issuers unable to operate seamlessly across borders, so global firms must issue through separate licensed entities in each jurisdiction. She urges the G20 to develop principles on regulatory equivalence, legal recognition of stablecoins for payments and collateral, and economic fungibility across four converging standards.

insights.claim: The GENIUS Act lets foreign issuers offer payment stablecoins in the US without a full license if Treasury deems their home regime comparable, but MiCA offers no equivalent pathway and requires issuers to be locally established and regulated.
insights.speaker: achhangani
insights.so_what: The asymmetry means US and EU stablecoin markets cannot be served by one entity, a structural cost for global issuers like Circle and Tether.

insights.claim: Global stablecoin companies must issue through two separate, locally licensed and regulated entities just to operate across the US and EU, duplicating issuer functions and absorbing added compliance and business costs.
insights.speaker: achhangani
insights.so_what: Duplicative licensing is a direct margin drag and barrier to scale for cross-border stablecoin issuers.
insights.quote: global stablecoin companies must issue through two separate, locally licensed and regulated entities—even to operate across the United States and the EU.

insights.claim: Both the GENIUS Act and MiCA require issuers to hold at least some reserves with local financial institutions, adding a practical hurdle for foreign issuers.
insights.speaker: achhangani
insights.so_what: Local reserve mandates fragment issuer balance sheets and raise the cost of operating in multiple jurisdictions.

insights.claim: Under the GENIUS Act, only payment stablecoins from US-based, GENIUS-licensed issuers can be treated as cash equivalents, used as derivatives margin or collateral, or accepted as a settlement asset by banks; foreign issuers do not qualify even with comparability determinations.
insights.speaker: achhangani
insights.so_what: Legal availability does not equal economic usability, so foreign stablecoins face a structural disadvantage in US institutional use cases.

insights.claim: MiCA takes an even harder line, prohibiting the offering, marketing, or distribution in the EU of stablecoins issued by non-EU entities altogether.
insights.speaker: achhangani
insights.so_what: The EU's outright ban on non-EU issuer distribution walls off a major market from US-based stablecoins.

insights.claim: For stablecoins issued under different regimes to be economically fungible, standards must converge in four areas: redemption rights, reserve composition, capital and liquidity requirements, and treatment of holders in resolution.
insights.speaker: achhangani
insights.so_what: A concrete four-part convergence checklist for assessing whether cross-border stablecoin interoperability is achievable.

insights.claim: A stablecoin reliably redeemable within two business days will be worth more than one that may take a week, so differences in redemption timing, pause conditions, or fees mean stablecoins under different regimes will not be economically equivalent.
insights.speaker: achhangani
insights.so_what: Redemption mechanics directly drive at-par value, meaning markets will price a discount into slower-redeeming tokens.
insights.quote: a stablecoin that can reliably be redeemed within two business days will be worth more than one that may take a week.

insights.claim: Bankruptcy and resolution regimes may treat home and host stablecoin holders differently, so holders of the same token could face different outcomes when things go wrong, and markets will price those differences ex ante.
insights.speaker: achhangani
insights.so_what: Resolution treatment is the hardest cross-border coordination problem and a hidden pricing risk in globally circulating stablecoins.

insights.claim: The Trump administration has made digital finance central to its economic agenda, identifying endorsement of a vibrant digital assets ecosystem and improved cross-border payments as policy priorities under the US G20 presidency.
insights.speaker: achhangani
insights.so_what: US presidency of the G20 gives stablecoin coordination unusual political momentum heading into the December Miami summit.
insights.locator: G20 finance ministers and central bankers

insights.claim: Massari argues the G20 should build on existing global stablecoin work to develop principles for regulatory equivalence, recognition for payments and settlement, and economic fungibility, while industry develops interoperability standards and infrastructure like stablecoin clearinghouses.
insights.speaker: achhangani
insights.so_what: Points to stablecoin clearinghouses and exchange facilities as emerging infrastructure opportunities if coordination advances.
